Cleaner edits cuts, cards and narration are cleaned up

Each clip starts and ends in a pause, with room for the transition, and starts on a sentence when it begins mid-sentence. The review marks every cut.

If the cards would squeeze the scenes, they are shortened after their voice and animation finish. The last gap is closed by holding or trimming a card, up to 12 % of the plug.

Trim: the silence before and after the speech, and every long pause or breath, is brought down to a short natural one — in the narration and in the title and end card voices. The other choice leaves the recording as it is unless a line would not fit its room.

Silence is trimmed first, and only where a line does not fit its room. If it still does not fit, the line starts under the end of the picture before it (a J-cut), by as much as it is short, up to 1.5 s. A line that runs past its clip carries on over the next picture (an L-cut) by itself. With the tune-in lines for both cards, the title card's is said from the title card and the end card's from the end card.

Start a script line with a time (00:03 VO: …) to put it there; each line is cut from the recording at word edges. Too long? Silence and pauses tighten, then the line leads its picture (J-cut), then up to 8 % faster, then optional lines go, then it ends on a word. Add (optional) to a line that can be dropped.

Each layer of a Photoshop file arrives in the style, over the promo, then holds. The bottom layer is treated as a backdrop and left out unless you keep it. Appears / Leaves below are not used; the style decides how each layer comes in, and it fades out at the end.

A PNG with transparency, a JPEG, or a Photoshop file (its visible layers are flattened, transparency kept), from the Animation artwork folder. It appears, holds, then leaves, over the finished promo — cards included. Holds for 0 means until the end.

These work independently — each has its own beat detection, and neither requires the other. Sync cuts to beat snaps the video's own cut points to the music's beat while scenes are being picked. Beat match instead adjusts the music's own tempo afterward to fit the cuts that already exist — it doesn't move or add any cuts itself. Turning on Beat match alone won't change where the video cuts at all; it only re-times the music. Using both together can leave cuts slightly off the beat they were synced to, since Beat match's own tempo-stretching shifts where those beats fall in the final mix.

    Parts are joined in this order and read as one episode, so the story can span them. A short never runs across the break between two parts.
    to

    A highlight reel joins the best scenes of the episode into one short. The length above is the length of the whole reel; each scene is found at about a fifth of it, the best-scoring ones are picked until the reel is full, and they play in episode order with a short fade between them. “Moments to find” becomes the number of reels: several reels never reuse a scene, and “Auto” makes one. Captions are burned into every scene.

    Mini-drama uses every stretch of the story, in order, none skipped. Billboards, credits, host and the other ticked material below are left out and the chapters carry on after them. Each chapter ends at the end of a spoken line, near a shot cut, at the strongest nearby beat. Each chapter opens with an EP n label and, when the next chapter follows on, closes with NEXT: EP n+1 ». “Moments to find”, “Focus” and “Avoid” do not apply.

    Say what is spoken and the captions and the choice of moments are more accurate than when Whisper guesses from the first seconds, which goes wrong on a programme that opens on music or mixes Filipino and English. Leave it on Auto-detect for a mix of languages.

    One model for both jobs keeps a single model on the GPU. Pick a separate story model only if you have a stronger text model pulled and the memory for both. Frames to rate is the number of vision calls for the whole video, however long it is — more is slower, not always better.

    Artwork Animation

    Artwork animations are made inside a project: the programme they are for. Create the project first — programme, program code, title, air date, a description and a picture — or open one, then make its animations there. Every animation you render for it is kept together in it, and everyone in the project’s group can play and download them.

    Create
    Saved animations

    Turns a schedule still into an 16:9 animation with a music bed. The artwork is drawn on frame by frame — its layers wipe, slide, fade or pop into place — not regenerated, so every title, date and time stays exactly as designed.

    Mode
    {% if allow_local_upload %}{% endif %}
    ✕
    {% if allow_local_upload %}{% endif %}
    ✕ With a storyboard, the AI model reads it next to the artwork and picks the style, timing and each layer’s animation. You see what it chose and why, and can change any of it.
    It is read as soon as it is picked: its layers, groups and pages are listed next, and you confirm what each one does.
    How to prepare a Photoshop file

    PNG, JPEG, TIFF or a Photoshop file, ideally 1920×1080. In a PSD, the bottom layer is the background and stays still; each top-level layer or group above it animates on its own — group the things that should move together, and name the layers so the direction can refer to them. Several schedule pages in one file: put each page’s rows in a top-level group named Page 1, Page 2, Page 3… They play in that order over the same background, and it does not matter which of them is showing or hidden when the file is saved.

    Pick the artwork, a length and optionally a music bed, then choose Generate animation. A 15-second animation takes well under a minute.
    Layers
    action safe 93%title safe 90%
    How this works

    A layered file is animated in three groups. The background (bottom layer) is static. The logo and schedule text only appear, the way the style says (wipe, fade, slide, pop) — then hold still, or breathe if you choose it — so they stay readable. Every other layer (shapes, ornaments, pictures) is on screen from the first frame and moves in a loop from the first frame to the last, in the style’s motion: mixed (layers take turns growing and shrinking, rotating left, rotating right), light sweep, gentle float, pulse, wobble, dancing, grow and shrink, rotate left or right. Logo and text layers are Photoshop text layers, groups that hold one, and layers with a word like logo, schedule, text, title, time, date or a day in their name — rename a layer to move it between groups; the result lists which layer went where. A flat picture has no separate layers: the whole picture arrives, and only the light sweep can run on it.

    How this works

    Changes whatever it names on top of the style. What it can say: wipe, slide, fade, pop or cut each layer in, from a direction (“from the left”, “bottom to top”); stop motion; fast or slow; light sweep, float, pulse, wobble, dance, grow and shrink, rotate left, rotate right, sway, move up, move down (both loop), rise / fall (one trip over the whole plug, no loop: a rising layer starts with its bottom edge on the bottom of the frame and ends with its top edge on the top of the frame; a falling one the reverse. A delay starts it later, a length on the layer shortens the trip), mixed or hold still for the moving layers. Name a layer to treat it differently, in how it appears or how it moves — this is also how to overrule the grouping for one layer (“title pops in, stars dance, logo breathes, ribbon holds still, burst pops in”).

    Music Generation — ACE-Step

    Generate
    Train LoRA

    Generate music on its own — for building a library of beds, restyling an existing track, or producing a sung stinger. Generated files can be saved into a show template from the Promo tab.

    Read live from your ACE-Step server. Pick a specific checkpoint (e.g. a fast/turbo model vs. a higher-quality one), or leave on the server default.

    Weight: 1.00

    Applies a fine-tuned style/voice on top of the base checkpoint. Drop trained checkpoints (.safetensors/.pt/.ckpt/.bin) into the server's configured LoRA folder (ACE_STEP_LORA_DIR) and refresh to see them here. Weight 1.0 is full strength; lower blends more of the base model back in.

    Comma-separated style tags work best — instrument, mood, era, production style.

    Leave empty and ACE-Step is told [inst] plus a vocal-suppressing negative prompt, which is the reliable way to guarantee no singing. Type lyrics here and both are dropped so the vocal actually comes through — use structure tags like [verse] and [chorus] on their own lines.

    What to steer away from. Leaving this empty on an instrumental take still applies a built-in vocal-suppressing default — type anything here (even just re-typing that same idea in your own words) to replace it entirely with your own.

    Reference strength: 0.50

    Generates in the shape of an existing track — useful for matching a show's established sting, or restyling a bed you already have. Higher strength stays closer to the reference; lower gives the prompt more freedom. Around 0.5 is a good starting point for a style transfer.

    ACE-Step reads the reference from a file path rather than an upload, so this needs ACE-Step running on this machine — or ACE_STEP_REF_DIR pointed at a mount both machines resolve identically.

    Duration (s): (blank = let ACE-Step pick) BPM: Key: Time signature: Samples: Steps: Seed:

    BPM, key, and time signature are all passed as prompt tags (ACE-Step conditions tempo/key/meter on the prompt text for this server rather than taking separate fields for them) — leaving any on auto lets the model pick what suits the style. More samples generate alternatives in one pass — slower, but you audition them side by side. Higher steps means better quality and proportionally more GPU time. Reuse a seed to reproduce a take.

    Runs an extra planning pass over your prompt and lyrics before generating, auto-filling in whatever you left on auto (tempo, key, structure). Slower — often better when you don't have strong opinions on the specifics above; leave it off for a fast, literal take on exactly what you typed.

    Advanced generation settings Server defaults ▸

    The actual quality/style controls ACE-Step's own pipeline exposes underneath the fields above. Left on "server default" (unchanged from before this existed) unless you set them. If your self-hosted output sounds different from a hosted service running the same checkpoint, this is usually why — a tuned service has picked deliberate values here.

    Guidance scale: Omega scale (APG):

    Guidance scale: how strictly the output follows your prompt/lyrics — ACE-Step's own default is 15; lower gives the model more creative freedom, higher can sound overcooked. Omega scale only matters when CFG type below is "apg" (default 10) — controls how fine-grained that guidance is.

    Scheduler: CFG type:

    ERG (Enhanced Realism Generation) settings — left unchecked here means "use the server's own default" for each, not "off". Check a box to explicitly force it on; ACE-Step's own pipeline defaults all three to on.

    Note: a turbo/distilled checkpoint ignores CFG guidance by design — if your ACE-Step server is running a turbo variant, guidance scale/CFG type/omega scale above may have no audible effect regardless of value.

    Set a prompt and duration, then hit Generate. Longer or multi-sample runs take proportionally longer — ACE-Step is polled for up to three minutes.

    Organizes a training dataset in the exact format ACE-Step's own dataset scanner expects, and kicks off/tracks a LoRA training run against it. One real gap this can't automate: turning your organized dataset into the "preprocessed tensors" training actually needs is a Gradio-UI-only step in ACE-Step itself (no REST/CLI equivalent exists) — you'll do that one step there, then come back here to start training.

    1. Dataset No dataset selected ▸

    A dataset is a named folder of tracks (audio + lyrics + caption). Create one, add tracks below, then hand its folder to ACE-Step's Gradio UI for tensor generation.

    2. Generate tensors (manual, in ACE-Step's Gradio UI) ▸

    In ACE-Step's own Gradio interface: load this dataset's folder (shown below once selected), run auto-labeling/review if needed, then "Generate Tensors" and save the output to the suggested path below (or wherever you prefer -- you'll paste the actual path into step 3).

    3. Start training ▸
    Rank (dim): Alpha: Learning rate: Epochs:
    Batch size: Save every N epochs:

    Defaults match ACE-Step's own documented defaults for whichever method is selected above.

    4. Progress & checkpoints ▸

    There's no live progress feed from ACE-Step for training -- this checks whether a checkpoint file has appeared and how long ago it last changed. Treat "likely finished" as a hint to go verify, not a guarantee.

    Text to SFX — Woosh

    Generate a one-shot sound effect from a plain description — for building a library of stingers and hits, or auditioning options before picking one for a show template. This is separate from the genre-based SFX the promo generator uses automatically at scene cuts.

    Be concrete: name the object and the action, not a mood. Woosh is a sound-effects model, not a music model — style words like "epic" or "cinematic" do less here than a literal description of the sound itself.

    Samples:

    No duration control -- Woosh has no such parameter itself, so this returns whatever length it naturally generates for the description rather than an artificially trimmed clip. More samples generate that many independent takes of the same description, so you can audition and pick the best one — each is a separate request to Woosh, run one after another.

    POST /api/trailer/generate  + vo_mode=tts & vo_text=<script> & vo_engine=fish_audio
GET  /api/voices                                  list the narration voices + languages
GET  /api/voices/tags                             Fish Audio delivery tags, in the right syntax
POST /api/vo/preview  + text, rate, language, engine, voice or ref_upload
POST /api/vo/preview  + full=1                    render a whole script, not an 800-char audition

    vo_engine picks the narration engine (defaults to fish_audio). There's no bundled default voice — every narration job needs either a voice picked from /api/voices or an uploaded reference sample to clone zero-shot (sent as a base64 references/reference_audio entry so speech is generated in that voice, no pre-registration required). The Narration section fetches the current engine's voice list live and reloads it if you switch engines; Fish Audio's list comes from the cloud API when FISH_AUDIO_API_KEY is set, and otherwise from a self-hosted server's /v1/references/list (falling back to /v1/models on older builds) — if a list comes back empty, upload a reference sample instead. You can also override the auto-detected language, and generate a short preview via /api/vo/preview before running the full plug job. Configured via env vars:

    FISH_AUDIO_URL
    self-hosted or api.fish.audio/v1/tts
    FISH_AUDIO_API_KEY
    blank for self-hosted
    FISH_AUDIO_MODEL
    s2.1-pro-free (cloud only)

    Docs

    Guides for the promo pipeline, tools, templates, and account settings. Pick a section on the left — content stays focused so you are not scrolling through everything at once.

    Workflow

    The Highlights Video page

    The page works in three steps: 1 Episode & settings, 2 Review the cut and 3 Result. You move on by themselves — a proposed cut opens the review, a finished plug opens the result — and any step you have been to can be reopened from the bar at the top. ← Settings and ← Back to settings return to the form with everything as you left it.

    Beside the form, Ready? says what is about to happen in one short list: the episode, the template (and that its settings are loaded), the length, genre and format, any steering, and the audio and cards chosen — and flags what is missing, such as no video yet, or AI Vision being unreachable (timecode cues do not need it). Use my last settings brings back the template, length, genre, format and steering of the last promo you started on this computer. The buttons stay at the bottom of the screen, with a one-line summary beside them, so they are never lost below a long form. Quick promo still hides the secondary controls; Advanced shows them all.

    Cleaner edits: cuts, cards and narration

    Three settings under Cleaner edits are on by default. Each can be switched off.

    • Cuts. Every clip starts and ends in a pause, never inside a word. The room before and after speech is sized to the transition, a clip that begins mid-sentence moves to the start of that sentence, and a hairline gap between two words is skipped for a real pause. Where the sound really stops is measured, not only taken from the transcript. Script timecode cues are your own exact points and stay as written. The review marks every clip Clean cut, Cut on a word (on a word edge but mid-sentence), Cut is tight or Cut mid-word, and summarises them at the top; drop or swap the risky ones.
    • Title & end cards. A card that would squeeze the scenes is shortened before scenes are chosen, but only after its own voice and its animation have finished (measured on the card itself); a card that is still moving at its last frame is left alone. The review shows each card’s length and what the scenes get. The last sliver of a gap is closed by holding or trimming a card up to 12 % of the plug (1 s minimum, 3.6 s on a 30 s plug); if the plug would still miss its exact length, the old 1 s last resort applies and the review says so. The Ready? panel shows the time budget as soon as you pick the card files, for example 15 s = title 6.0 + end card 6.0 + scenes 3.0.
    • Uploaded narration. The recording is read with speech-to-text. Start a script line with a time to place it there — 00:03 VO: Abangan ngayong gabi, [0:07.5] ... or @12.5s ... — and each line is found in the recording and cut at word edges, so one recording with several lines can be placed at several points. Lines without a time follow the previous one with the pause the speaker left. If it is too long for the room it has, it is fitted in this order: silence and pauses tighten (down to 0.15 s), then the line is brought forward under the picture before it (a J-cut, up to 1.5 s, as much as it is short, and only then), the speech speeds up by at most 8 % (pitch kept), lines marked (optional) are dropped from the end, and as the very last step the end is trimmed at a word edge. A line the recording does not contain is reported, not guessed. With no times in the script, a recording that fits plays exactly as before. The review lists every line with its time and status. AI-voice (text-to-speech) narration is unchanged.

    What happens, in order, from upload to finished export:

    Amber dashed = optional, feeds into the main pipeline rather than sitting inline with it.

    1. Scene detection — PySceneDetect (Content or Adaptive) finds every cut, using the same settings as the Scene Search tool.
    2. Rating — sharpness/brightness/duration/faces (OpenCV), AI Vision quality, and dialogue boosts from faster-whisper.
    3. Beat/dialogue prep (optional) — beat grid and word-level timestamps when those options are on.
    4. Scene selection — highest-rated scenes fill the target duration with spacing, beat/word snaps, and top-up passes.
    5. Assembly — scenes plus title/end cards with the genre transition (or custom matte).
    6. Audio normalize — SOT loudness baseline for later mix steps.
    7. SFX at cuts — Woosh from the genre prompt; procedural fallback only mid-job if Woosh fails.
    8. Background music — ACE-Step or upload, normalized and ducked under SOT.
    9. Narration (optional) — Fish Audio or uploaded VO, normalized before mix.
    10. Final mix — sidechain ducking, gap-aware BGM dips, optional dual-mono, loudness pass.
    11. Export — MP4, ProRes, or AVC-Intra-style packages.

    Jobs use a concurrency-limited queue (default 2) so local model servers are not overloaded. Position in queue is shown while waiting.

    Vertical Shorts

    Cuts a long-form programme into stand-alone 9:16 shorts (1080×1920 H.264, AAC, −14 LUFS unless another Audio level is chosen). It is separate from the promo generator and does not change how a plug is built; it shares the same services, job queue and network folders.

    1. Find moments

    Open the episode’s project (see Projects below), go to Create shorts, pick the full episode and choose Preview the cut. Nothing is rendered in this step. Generate without preview runs the same analysis and then renders every moment it found, with the Output settings, as one job; the moments are still listed afterwards so any can be re-timed and rendered again.

    Length of each short starts at 60 to 120 seconds. Moments to find is a ceiling — up to 5, 8, 12, 20, 50 or 100 — or Auto. A number keeps the best that many, weak ones included if there is room. Auto has no number: it keeps every distinct moment the story model rates {{ shorts_auto_min_story }}/10 or better (100 at most), and if none reaches that it lists everything it found and says so. An episode only holds so many: two moments may share up to half their length, so 45 minutes at 60–120 s yields a few dozen at most whatever is asked for. Each five-minute stretch of dialogue is asked for as many moments as it can hold end to end, eight at the very most. One render takes up to 100 shorts.

    Billboards, credits, narration and the like are never in a moment. A broadcast episode or a movie carries material that is not the drama: opening and closing billboards (OBB/CBB) and sponsor reads, opening titles and end credits, a narrator or voice-over telling the story, a host speaking to the audience, recaps (sa nakaraang) and teasers (abangan), and black between acts. The story model marks the lines that are any of these, and the AI Vision model says of every frame it rates whether it is the drama, credits or a title card, a logo or billboard, a host, or black — for the frames across the whole video and again for those inside each moment. A frame stands for its shot (up to 8 seconds either side of it), and non-drama frames less than 20 seconds apart with no drama between them are taken as one run, as credits are. No moment includes any of it: a moment that runs into one keeps its longest clean stretch of lines (marked Trimmed clear), is never lengthened into one, and its lead-in, tail and padding stop at its edge; one with too little left is dropped. A note above the list says what was left out and where. Spoken language tells Whisper what is being said instead of letting it guess from the first seconds, which is the biggest single gain in caption accuracy (a deployment that is nearly always one language can set SHORTS_LANGUAGE, e.g. tl, to start the form on it; leave Auto-detect for mixed speech). Names and terms are handed to Whisper as context so characters and places are spelled as written. Leave out these parts of the video takes ranges of your own — 0:00-1:45, 44:05-end — for anything they miss. Something left out by mistake can be added back with Add your own moment, which is never trimmed.

    What should these shorts feature is a preference: matching moments are favoured, but a weak one is not picked just for matching. What should these shorts avoid is a rule: a moment mainly about it, or showing it, is left out however strong. Both are judged by the story model from the dialogue and the visual notes, so neither applies when a fallback had to be used (a warning says so).

    • How it looks. A bounded number of frames, spread across the whole video, are rated 1–5 by the AI Vision model for visible drama. Once the moments are proposed, up to four more frames inside each are rated too (160 in all at most, skipping any already rated), so a moment is judged on its own pictures and not on wherever the first sample happened to fall. Half as many moments again as you asked for are looked at this way, and the closer look decides which make the list.
    • How it sounds. The episode’s sound level is read once. A moment gets a Sound score (shown out of 10; 5 is an ordinary stretch of this programme) from how loud it gets against the episode as a whole and how much of it rises well above the usual — a raised voice, laughter, a slam. It counts for a little in the total, less than pace.
    • What it means. The dialogue is transcribed, and a story model reads it in overlapping five-minute stretches — with those visual notes placed in line — and proposes moments that stand on their own: a setup, a turn, a payoff.
    • Where it cuts. Each proposal is fitted to your length range, then its in and out points are moved so they never fall inside a spoken word and land on a shot change when one is close. Too long, it loses its opening lines, never its ending. Finally both ends are checked against the sound itself, since a transcript’s word times are a guess and per-line times only approximate: an out point that lands while a word is still sounding is moved to where it stops (up to 0.8 s later, or the gap between two words where speech runs straight on), and an in point that lands inside a word is moved back to where that word starts — never into the line before, past the maximum length or under the minimum. Over a wall of music, where a word cannot be told from a gap, the ends stay where they were. Too short, it is given the lines around it — first without crossing a pause of more than 6 seconds, then, if it has to, pauses of up to 10 — and then up to 6 seconds of the quiet before and after it. The minimum is a minimum: a moment that still falls short of it is left out, and a note above the list says how many were. (If every moment found falls short, they are listed as they are, marked Short.)
    • Lines timed to the line only. A speech-to-text service that returns times for whole lines rather than words — often rounded to the second — leaves every caption and cut point up to a second out. When that is what came back and the times are rounded to the second (most of them sharing one fraction of a second, as in 0:30.29, 0:32.29, 0:33.29), the episode’s sound is read once and each line is moved onto where its sound really starts and stops: a line given a start in silence begins where the sound does, one given a start in the middle of sound began where that sound started, and the same for its end. Over a wall of music or a crowd, where speech cannot be told from a gap, a line keeps its times. A note above the list says how many lines were moved. A service that returns word timings is still better: captions then change with the words.
    • When a line was really spoken. A speech-to-text service places the end of a line well, but after a stretch with no speech it often gives the line the start of that stretch as its own: three words timed as lasting thirty seconds. Left alone, that line’s caption comes up half a minute before anyone speaks, and a short that opens on it opens on dead air. So a line timed as lasting far longer than its words could take (more than double, and by more than 3 seconds) is taken to have ended where it says and started as late as its words allow. A line that really is delivered slowly is left as timed.

    Each candidate's score (0–100) weighs story most, then visual drama, then dialogue pace, then sound. Both Ollama and faster-whisper must be reachable; the job refuses to start otherwise rather than choose on half the evidence. The same goes for a transcription that fails part-way (the service errors or times out): the job stops and says why. Only a source with genuinely nothing to hear — no audio track, or no speech in it — falls back to picture alone. A warning above the list tells you when a fallback was used (no story found, or no dialogue at all). The speech-to-text service has to return timings as well as text: it is asked for verbose_json with timestamps and, if it answers that with the text alone, for srt and then vtt, which every Whisper server can write. Subtitle timings are per line, not per word, so captions made that way change a line at a time. A server that gives no timings in any of the three stops the job with a message saying so. On a master that keeps its sound on separate tracks or channels (eight mono tracks, say, with the full mix on 3 and 4), the dialogue is looked for where there is sound rather than on the first track: silent channels are never sent, a stereo pair recorded out of phase is sent as one side, and if the first candidate has no speech in it the next is tried, up to four. A note above the list says which track the dialogue was read from, and the shorts and their previews take their sound from the same place. When nothing is found, the warning lists what was tried and at what level.

    2. Review

    The page works in three steps, shown along the top: 1 Source (the episode, lengths, language and Output settings), 2 Moments and 3 Export (the finished shorts). Moments is a workspace. On the left is the list of moments, best first or in episode order, each with a thumbnail, its in–out, length and score (green 75 and over, amber 50 and over); the tick decides whether it is rendered, and clicking a row selects it. In the middle is a 9:16 player: it plays the real clip with its sound and shows the captions the moment will get, as they will be burned in (a correction made in Captions shows at once). Set In here and Set Out here take the in or out point from the picture’s position; Exact 9:16 preview renders a small copy with the framing, corrections and captions applied. On the right the editor has four tabs: Trim (title, in and out typed as m:ss.s or seconds, or nudged by ±0.1 and ±1 s), Captions, Framing and Dialogue. Under them, the whole episode is drawn as a timeline of its moments (ticked ones solid, unticked hatched, the selected one outlined, the joins between parts marked) and, below it, the selected moment with its surroundings, where the two ends can be dragged. A moment can be made longer as well as shorter: type a new in or out, nudge it, drag an end, or tick show 5 s beyond the ends under the player, which plays a little before and after the moment so Set In here / Set Out here can reach past where it ends now. The Length of each short you set on Source only steers which moments are found; what you may trim to is 3 seconds up to 5 minutes, and a change outside that is refused (a moment that already breaks it may not be made worse). The bar at the bottom stays in view: total running time, a summary of the Output settings (open them there, with presets — Standard, Two-person scenes and Whole frame), and Render. A finished render lights up Export and is offered in the queue as Show the shorts; it never takes the editor away from you. Keys, when you are not typing in a box: Space play or pause, ↑ ↓ previous or next moment, I and O set in and out at the playhead, X tick or untick. The player shows the source framing; reframing happens at render, and the exact preview shows it.

    The Framing tab shows each of its shots as a still, with the 9:16 window drawn where it will be: dashed for what was worked out, solid for a correction. For any shot, choose Crop here and slide the window (or click the still where it should go), Whole frame to show the whole picture over a blurred copy, or Split screen to stack the two people of the shot, one above the other (offered only for a shot with exactly two people far enough apart to give each a pane; the panes are drawn on the still, numbered top to bottom, and every split in a clip shares one window size). Make vertical preview renders a small 9:16 copy of the moment as it will come out — framing, corrections and captions — in a few seconds, without spending a full render. Use this framing keeps the corrections with that moment (marked framing set); a corrected shot is framed that way for its whole length, even where the plan had followed someone, cut between speakers or split the screen. The corrections belong to the shots, not to the in and out points: move those afterwards and each correction stays on the shot it was made for. Back to automatic drops them.

    The Captions tab opens the lines it will be captioned with, exactly as they will appear: change the wording, change when a line is on screen (times are from the start of the short, to a hundredth of a second), empty a line to drop it, or add one. Use these captions keeps them with that moment — it is marked captions edited — and they are what is burned in and written to its .srt. Moving the in or out point afterwards does not lose them: the lines still inside the new range stay, moved to where they now fall, and whatever the range gained at either end gets the automatic captions. Back to automatic drops the corrections. A phone-shaped preview beside the lines shows the line as it is burned in (size, outline and position) and follows what you do: click or type in a line and it shows that line; drag the slider to any point of the short. Play plays the real clip with its sound, a few seconds after the editor opens (while it is prepared the preview is stills and a clock), and the line on screen follows the picture’s own clock, so each caption is shown with its voice. Captions are timed from the words: when an analysis is made the first word after a silence is moved to where the speech really begins, so a caption does not come up early and wait for the voice. Beside a line, Split cuts it in two at the text cursor (the time is divided in proportion), Join runs it into the next; in a time box the up and down keys move it by 0.05 s (Shift: 0.5 s). A line longer than fits on one line at the chosen size is marked amber and the preview shows it wrapped. One caption is on screen at a time, so where two lines overlap the earlier one ends as the next begins.

    Your review is saved as you make it — ticks, titles, in and out points, corrected captions and framing, and moments added by hand. The analysis and the review are kept on the server (in shorts_analyses next to the library; SHORTS_ANALYSES_DIR to put them elsewhere) for 14 days after they were last opened (SHORTS_ANALYSIS_DAYS), so a restart or a day away does not mean analysing the episode again. Earlier cuts of this project, at the top of Create shorts, lists them with Open, which brings the cut back as it was left, and Delete, which removes the analysis and its review but never shorts made from it. You see your own; admins see everyone’s.

    The episode itself is a staged copy and is still cleared from the server after a while and on a restart. If it was picked from a network folder, the analysis remembers where: the review offers Fetch the episode again, which previews and framing need, and a render fetches it by itself. An episode uploaded from a computer cannot be fetched again; pick it again and re-analyse.

    3. Render

    • Auto reframes shot by shot: it crops to the face or faces, follows a subject that really moves, and for a shot where two similar-sized faces are too far apart to fit a vertical frame it shows the whole picture over a blurred copy of itself rather than cut someone out. Who a shot is of is worked out from the whole shot, not frame by frame: a face counts as a person when it is found in the same place in at least 30% of the frames that show any face, and a person the detector loses for a moment (a turned head, hair, a passing hand) is taken to be where they were last seen. So the window is centred on the people in the shot and stays there. When the faces do not fit together but one is clearly nearer the camera (1.6 times the area of the next), the shot is of that person and the crop is centred on them. A shot with no face in it — someone seen from behind, side-on or looking down — is searched for head and shoulders instead; if the same figure, large enough to be who the shot is of, is found in at least 40% of its frames, the crop follows them. Failing that, the crop goes where the picture is in focus: drama keeps its subject sharp and the background soft, so the sharpest part of the frame is usually the person. That is used only when it is clear — the sharpest stretch at least 1.3 times as sharp as the average, in at least 40% of the shot’s frames, and in much the same place each time. A picture sharp all over, as in a deep-focus wide shot, is centre-cropped. Anything worked out wrong can be corrected under Framing….
    • Split screen is Auto with a different answer for those wide two-shots: when the shot is exactly two people, each gets half the frame — the one on the left on top, the one on the right below — and captions move to the join between them. Each half is tightened until the other person's face is out of it. A shot with three or more faces, or two it cannot separate cleanly, is shown whole as in Auto.
    • Always crop fills the screen on every shot and commits to one side of a wide two-shot. Fit always shows the whole picture.
    • Follow the speaker (off unless ticked) changes only those wide two-shots: it cuts between close framings of whoever is talking, holding each for at least a second or so and changing just before the next line. It decides from how much each mouth moves while the transcript says words are being spoken. Where it cannot tell — nobody speaking, a face turned away, two mouths moving alike — the shot is reframed exactly as it would be with the option off. With Split screen it works the other way round: the screen is split while both people talk, and a shot where only one of them talks is framed on that one.
    • Captions are burned in from the transcript a few words at a time, and an .srt is saved next to each MP4.
    • Format is the file each short is delivered as: MP4 (H.264 High Profile), or Apple ProRes 422 HQ at 29.97 or 23.976 fps. A ProRes short is rendered to H.264 first, at higher quality than an ordinary MP4 short, and the .mov is made from that by the same export step the other tabs use; the MP4 is kept as the copy that plays here. Download, Download all and Send hand over the .mov. ProRes 422 HQ is roughly 1.3–1.7 GB per minute at 1080×1920, so a large batch needs the disk for it. AVC-Intra 100 is not offered here: it is a 1920×1080 format.
    • Audio level is how loud each short is overall (integrated loudness): −14 LUFS unless you choose otherwise, which is what online video is levelled to; −23 (EBU R128) and −24 (ATSC A/85) are there for shorts going to air. The true peak stays under −1.5 dBTP. A short rendered again for new captions keeps the level it had.
    • Ending is how every short in the render finishes. Cut on the last frame stops where the moment stops. Cliffhanger stops the action dead on the moment’s last beat and holds it for 2 seconds (the Hold for box sets any length from 0.5 to 8 s; the server default is SHORTS_CLIFF_HOLD) while the picture pushes in by 3%, takes on a cooler, higher-contrast grade and darkens slightly at the corners; then it cuts straight to black. That adds the hold plus 0.4 s of black to each short (2.4 s by default), and no caption is drawn over the hold. A Sound effect picked from the SFX folder with Browse library comes in the instant the picture stops and goes out with the black; Level raises or lowers it in dB. It is mixed in after the dialogue has been levelled and limited so it cannot clip, and a copy is kept with the batch so a short can be re-captioned later. A Transition overlay picked from the Transitions folder with Browse library (a video with transparency: ProRes 4444 or QuickTime Animation .mov, or VP9 .webm) plays over the picture, centred on the instant it freezes, scaled to fit with its transparency kept; its sound, if it has one, is mixed in, and it is cut off at the black. It is kept with the batch too. If ffmpeg cannot read it, the short is rendered without it. Fade the last short to black is for the last episode of a series: the final short of the render (the last moment in the episode) fades out — picture, captions and sound, over 0.3–3 s — instead of cutting or holding, while every other short keeps the Ending chosen. It adds no time, so its last words fade with the picture; trim its Out point a little earlier if that matters.
      • The picture. The moment plays to its last frame; the hold is made from what comes just after the out point. It is not a single still when it can help it: if those next frames are nearly motionless (someone standing in a close-up), up to 0.16 s of them is played forwards and back in extreme slow motion, which keeps the breathing, hair and cloth barely alive while the pose and expression stay locked. If anything is really moving in them (a gesture, a camera move) it holds one frame, because looping real movement would show as a wobble. Only when the out point is on a cut, or at the very end of the file, is the hold made from the moment’s own last frames instead. Nothing is generated: every held frame comes from the footage.
      • The sound is not cut where the transcript says the last word ends — that time is early as a rule, and with per-line timings only approximate. The sound around the out point is measured instead. If a word is still being spoken there, it is let finish under the held picture, up to 0.8 s, and stops in the pause that follows. If speech runs straight on into the next line, the sound stops in the gap between the two words nearest the out point, with a very short fade. If the out point is already in a pause, it stops there. Where the level cannot tell a word from a gap (a wall of music, a crowd), it stops at the out point. Whatever happens, the last half second of the hold and the black are silent.

    Batches are kept in their project until deleted: play, download one or all (.zip), or send to a video network destination.

    Running times. The bottom of the review list gives the source’s total running time (TRT) and the TRT of the moments ticked, as they are ticked and re-timed (before any cliffhanger hold). Each batch ends with its source TRT and the TRT of its shorts, and the bottom of Shorts in this project totals them by source — every short made from that episode, across all its batches — with the share of the source they come to. Batches rendered before this was added did not record their source’s TRT, so only their shorts’ is shown.

    Changing captions on a saved short

    Captions on a saved short opens the same editor on that short’s lines. What saving does depends on where the captions are:

    • Burned into the picture: saving renders that one short again with the corrected lines — same framing, same ending, same file names — and replaces it once the new files are complete. It takes about as long as the short took the first time. If the render fails, or the file is open in a player or still downloading (Windows will not replace it), the short is left exactly as it was.
    • Not burned in (rendered with Burn in captions off): saving rewrites the .srt and is immediate.
    • Burned in, but the episode has gone from the server: staged files are cleared after a while ({{ '%g'|format(upload_ttl_hours) }} hours unused, by default), and the picture cannot be rendered again without the episode. The editor says so, and saving updates the .srt only. The same applies to shorts rendered before this was added. To change what is in the picture, analyse the episode again.

    Anyone who can see a batch can read its captions; changing them is for whoever rendered it and admins, like deleting it.

    Projects

    Shorts are filed by project: the episode they are cut from. A project records the programme title, episode, air date, a description and a thumbnail (JPEG, PNG or WebP up to 8 MB; until one is given the project shows a frame of its newest short). A project is the only way in: choose New project, or open one, and its page has two views — Shorts in this project, every batch rendered for it, and Create shorts, the form that makes more. There is no way to start a job outside a project, so nothing is saved loose. A new project opens on Create shorts. Jobs are queued: start Preview the cut, Generate without preview or Render again while another is running and it is added to the Queue under the buttons, each with its own progress and Cancel. The server runs as many at once as its job limit allows (the same limit as Highlights Video) and the rest show Waiting. A finished cut opens by itself only if no cut is open for that project; otherwise the queue offers Open the review or Show the shorts, going to its project first. Every cut is also kept under Earlier cuts. The queue lives in the page: reloading it forgets the list (the jobs go on, see Jobs), so reopen finished cuts from Earlier cuts.

    A project belongs to the group of whoever created it — always their current group: nobody picks it, and if the creator moves to another group, their projects move with them. Everyone in that group with access to Vertical Shorts sees the project and can play, download and send what is in it; other groups do not see it at all. Someone in several groups sees the projects of all of them. Admins see every project. Deleting a batch, or moving it to another project, is for whoever rendered it and admins. A project can be deleted by whoever created it or an admin, and only once it is empty: deleting a project never deletes shorts. Shorts rendered before projects existed are listed under Not in a project for their maker, with Move to to file them.

    Limits worth knowing

    • Candidates are proposals. A local model can misjudge what stands alone — preview before rendering.
    • One continuous stretch per short; it does not assemble a short from separate scenes, and adds no music, titles or graphics.
    • Follow the speaker reads mouth movement, not voices. It can pick the wrong person when a listener laughs, chews or mouths along while someone else talks, and it cannot follow a speaker who is off screen or facing away. Check wide two-shots before publishing, and render again with it unticked if one is wrong.
    • Face tracking uses OpenCV's built-in Haar cascades unless a YuNet model file is supplied. The cascades miss many profile, tilted, lowered and small faces, and a shot with no detected face is centre-cropped, wherever the person in it is standing — this is the commonest reason for a crop that is not on anyone. Advanced, on the create form, says which detector this server is using; where it is the Haar cascades, an admin sees Download the YuNet face model there. That fetches face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx (about 230 KB, MIT licence) from the OpenCV model zoo on GitHub, checks it is exactly the published file, and puts it in a models folder next to the app, where it is used from the next render. A server with no internet access can be given the same file by hand, or SHORTS_FACE_MODEL pointed at it.
    • Captions are only as well timed as the transcript. A service that returns word timings gives captions that change with the words; one that returns only lines (the subtitle fallback) gives captions that change a line at a time, and if its times are to the whole second they can be up to a second early or late.

    Reading the episode where it is

    (Highlights Video and the Player have the same switch on the Video (HIRES) folder.)

    By default, picking an episode from Browse library copies it to the server first. Under Config > Network, switch on Read files in place for the Vertical Shorts, Video (HIRES), Title card or End card folder and nothing is copied: the episode is analysed and rendered straight from the share, so there is no wait and no extra disk use. The account PRISM runs under must be able to open the share path itself (the login in Config is only used for browsing and copying); when it cannot, that pick is copied as before and says so on its chip. PRISM only reads the file — it never changes or deletes it — but the share has to stay reachable while you work on the project, and analyses and renders go at the speed of the share.

    Episodes in more than one part

    If the episode comes as several files (up to ten), add them under This episode comes in more than one part. The parts are laid end to end and read as one episode: the story model sees the whole thing, so a setup in part 1 can pay off in part 2, and the sound and picture are rated against the whole programme. A short is always cut from one part — it never runs across the break — and each moment shows which part it is in, with its times read within that part. To leave something out, name the part: part 2 0:00-1:45, part 3 18:10-end (a range with no part means part 1). Shorts are numbered in episode order across all the parts, and the total running time counts every part.

    POST /api/shorts/analyze  + shorts_file_network, (shorts_file2_network ... shorts_file10_network), min_dur, max_dur, count, focus?, avoid?
                          + auto_render=1, reframe, speaker, subtitles, subtitle_size  (render every moment found, no review)
GET  /api/shorts/progress/<job_id>
GET  /api/shorts/analysis/<analysis_id>
POST /api/shorts/render   {analysis_id, items:[{start,end,title}], reframe: auto|split|crop|fit, speaker?, subtitles}
GET  /api/shorts/batches
POST /api/shorts/batches/<id>/send   {destination_id, include_srt?, files?, filename?}
GET  /api/shorts/projects                      POST: title, episode?, air_date?, description?, thumbnail? (file)
POST /api/shorts/projects/<id>   (same fields; remove_thumbnail=1)        DELETE when empty
POST /api/shorts/batches/<id>/project   {project_id}
POST /api/shorts/analyze now also needs project_id

    Order and numbering

    Shorts are numbered in the order their moments happen in the episode, not by score and not by the order they were ticked: …_short_01_… is the earliest moment and the highest number the latest, so a folder sorted by name, the zip and a destination all read in story order. Each short in a batch shows that number on its picture and where in the episode it comes from. In the list of moments, List in switches between episode order (the default) and best first, and each ticked moment shows the number its short will get (“Short 3 of 8”); unticking one renumbers the rest. A short that fails to render leaves its number unused. Batches saved before this are also listed in episode order, though their filenames keep the numbers they were given.

    Sending

    Send all at the top of a batch copies every short (and its captions) to a video destination set up under Config > Network, under the names they have. Each short also has its own Send…: it opens a destination and a filename box, filled in with the short’s current name, and nothing is sent until you press Send there — change the name first to rename the file as it goes out. The extension stays the file’s own, spaces become underscores, and the short’s .srt goes with it under the same name. The saved short keeps its original name, and a file of the same name already at the destination is replaced.

    Artwork Animation

    Turns one schedule still into an 16:9 animation of 10, 15, 20 or 30 seconds with a music bed, in any of the delivery formats the promo generator offers.

    The workspace

    The page works in three steps: 1 Artwork, 2 Layers & animation and 3 Result. The artwork is read as soon as it is picked (from Browse library, or from this computer where that is allowed) and the layers step opens: every top-level layer and group of the PSD, top of the stack first, as Photoshop lists them, each with a thumbnail, its kind, and the part it will play — Background (the bottom layer, and anything that covers the whole picture over it: still), Page n (a group named as a page, with how many rows it breaks into), Logo & text (a text layer, or one named like a logo or the schedule: appears, then holds or breathes), Moving (everything else), or Hidden / Left out. A layer that was switched off in the file is listed and left out. The picture in the middle shows the artwork as it will rest, one tab per page, with the selected layer outlined; the line under it counts what is background, pages, logo and text, and moving layers.

    Select a layer and What should it do? lets you correct it: make it the Background (it and everything below it become the still backdrop), Logo or schedule text, Moving decoration, a schedule page (with its page number), or leave it out; As detected goes back. The list is read again after each change, so the counts and the page tabs show what will be drawn. A group shows the layers inside it.

    Split into its layers opens a group: its layers are listed beneath it, indented, and each is sorted on its own — a header group can hold a background group (choose its last layer as Background to keep the whole stack still), the logo, and ornaments that move. Put the group back together undoes it. For any layer that is not the background, Animation of this layer sets how it Arrives (wipe, slide, fade, pop or appear at once, with a direction) and what it does Then: hold still, light sweep, float, pulse, wobble, shake, grow and shrink, rotate left or rotate right, sway, dance, move up, move down or breathe. What you set on a layer wins over the style and the prompt; Back to the style removes it. On a page it applies to every row of that page.

    The Animation tab holds the length, style, how logo and text behave and the extra direction; Music & file the delivery format, the music and its level. Generate animation in the bar below draws it with your corrections, and the plug opens in step 3. A Photoshop file that has to be animated as one flat picture (blend modes, effects) shows as one layer with the reason above the list.

    Easy and Advanced

    The Mode switch at the top right chooses how much you see. Easy (the default) reads the artwork, says in one short list what will happen — this stays still, these pages come one after another, these appear and hold, these keep moving — and lists anything worth checking in plain words: text outside the title-safe area (the outer 5% a television may cut off), text too small to read on a television, pages that would go by too fast. Then it asks only for a length (the server suggests one from the number of pages and rows, and picks it for you until you choose another), a style (shown as cards, each marked Calm or Lively) and the music. Advanced adds the layer list, per-layer roles, Split into its layers for groups, and the controls below.

    Preview the animation draws the first seconds small and silent in a few seconds, so you see the style move before the full render; change the style, length or a layer and it redraws by itself. The preview has the player’s own scrubber, ◀ frame and frame ▶ to step one frame at a time, and Safe areas to overlay the action-safe (93%) and title-safe (90%) rectangles. Words in Extra direction are read by keyword only in the preview; the full render may use the AI model.

    Timing (under the style) is One after another by default: the layers come in in turn and their loops run a beat apart. All together, same timing brings every layer in on the same beat and moves them in step (pulse included); the extra direction understands it too (“all together”, “at the same time”; “one by one” to switch it off). A layer given its own Starts later by still keeps it.

    Timing & feel (Advanced, in This layer) gives one layer its own Starts later by (a moving layer given a delay then arrives, instead of being there from the first frame), Takes (how long it comes in), Eases (settle gently, smooth in and out, overshoot a little, even) and Strength of the motion (below 1 gentler, above 1 bigger — shake, rotate, float and the rest). On a page, Gap between its rows sets how far apart its rows come in. A group animates as one piece until it is split; split, each of its layers can be staggered with Starts later by.

    Saved looks. Save this look keeps the style, length, extra direction, format and everything set on layers — roles, split groups, arrival, motion, timing — by layer name, so it fits next week’s file if its layers are named the same. Picking a look applies it and says which of its layers this file does not have. Looks are shared with the team: anyone can use one, only the person who made it (or an admin) can delete or replace it. Export and Import move a look as a small file between servers. Same as last time is always your own latest settings.

    The same look for more files. After an animation is made, The same look for more files on the result step lists other artwork from Browse library and makes each with the same style, length, music and format, matched to the look by layer name, one after another. Each finished animation is added to the results and to Saved animations, with the per-layer settings used.

    Why it is drawn, not generated

    A schedule is text: titles, dates, times. A video model repaints every pixel of every frame, so that text would come back warped. Here each layer's own pixels are moved, faded or uncovered, so the logo and the text come to rest exactly as designed.

    Artwork

    • Flat image (PNG, JPEG, TIFF): animated as one picture.
    • Layered Photoshop file: the bottom layer is the static background; each visible top-level layer or group above it animates on its own, lowest first. Group the things that should arrive together and give layers plain names (“Title”, “Schedule Mon”) so the prompt can refer to them. More than twelve top-level layers: the lowest are merged into the background.
    • Layers must be plain pixels in Normal mode. If the file uses blend modes, layer effects, clipping or adjustment layers at the top level, it is animated as one flat picture instead and the result says so — merge or rasterise those layers to get layer-by-layer animation.
    • Design at 1920×1080. Other shapes are shown whole with black around them, never cropped.

    Several pages in one file

    For a schedule too long for one screen, keep one PSD: the background, the ornaments, the logo and the day stay as ordinary layers, and each page’s rows go into a top-level group whose name begins with Page and a number — Page 1, Page 2 afternoon, PAGE-3 (Pg 1 and P1 work too).

    • The name is what makes a group a page. Any other group (a header holding the logo and the day, say) stays on screen for the whole plug.
    • Pages play in the order of their numbers, wherever they sit in the layer stack, and whether they are showing or hidden when the file is saved — so you can work with one page visible at a time. A layer hidden inside a page stays hidden.
    • Everything on screen throughout behaves as usual. Each page’s rows then appear top to bottom the way the style says, hold, and fade away for the next page; the last page stays to the end. Whatever sits on one line (a time and its title) arrives together, however the page is layered.
    • The time left once the logo and day are in is shared equally between the pages. Three pages want 20 or 30 seconds: the result warns when a page is complete on screen for less than three seconds.
    • The pages need a background layer of their own beneath them. Everything inside a page group counts as schedule text: it appears and leaves with its page and does not take the moving layers’ motion.

    Animation style and direction

    A layered file is animated in three groups:

    • Background — the bottom layer, plus any layers directly above it that cover the whole picture (a texture, a gradient). Static, on screen from the first frame. It never animates unless the direction says “fade in the background”.
    • Logo and schedule text — Photoshop text layers, groups that hold a text layer, and layers with a word such as logo, schedule, text, title, time, date, program, show or a day (Mon, Tuesday) in their name. They appear one after another, lowest first, the way the style says; afterwards they hold still or, if chosen, breathe (swell and settle by under two percent, all together). They are at rest, exactly as designed, on the last frame.
    • Every other layer — shapes, pictures, ornaments. On screen from the first frame and moving in a loop from the first frame to the last, without easing in or out.

    The result lists which layer went into which group. If a layer landed in the wrong one, rename it in Photoshop (rasterised text called “Layer 5” will be taken for an ornament and will move), or name it in the direction. A file with nothing but logo and text above the background has nothing left to keep moving, and the result says so.

    The Animation style dropdown picks the combination: how the logo and text appear + how the other layers move — Wipe reveal + grow, rotate left, rotate right (mixed), where the moving layers take those three motions in turn (the default), Fade in + light sweep, Wipe reveal + light sweep, Slide up + gentle float, Pop in + pulse one by one, Stop motion wipe + wobble, Pop in + dancing (a hop on every beat with a lean and a swell), Pop in + grow and shrink, Fade in + rotate left, Fade in + rotate right, or Fade in + hold still for no motion at all after the build. A rotating layer tilts up to twelve degrees and comes back; long layers turn less so their ends do not swing into their neighbours. A flat picture arrives whole from black; only the light sweep can run on it, because the other motions would move its background.

    Extra direction is optional and changes whatever it names on top of the style: wipe, slide, fade, pop or cut, from a direction; stop motion; a slow push in (this one moves the whole frame, background included); fast or slow; light sweep, float, pulse, wobble, dance, grow and shrink, rotate left, rotate right, sway, mixed or hold still for the moving layers. Name a layer to give it its own arrival or its own motion, whatever group it is in (“stars dance, logo breathes, ribbon holds still, burst pops in”). The words are matched directly and, when Ollama is reachable, also read by the AI model so it can tell which named layer an instruction is about. Each result states the style and how the direction was understood.

    Music

    Optional, from the Music network folder. Trimmed to the length with a fade out, looped if shorter, and levelled to the Audio level chosen for the plug. That menu starts on the loudness target under Config > Production and offers the usual ones: −14 LUFS for online video, −23 (EBU R128) or −24 (ATSC A/85) for broadcast. The level is the loudness of the whole plug measured over its length, not a peak; the true-peak ceiling stays the one under Config > Production. A saved plug says what it was levelled to.

    Setup

    Set the artwork folder under Config > Network > Animation artwork. Photoshop files need the psd-tools package on the server.

    POST /api/schedule/render   + schedule_image_network, duration (10|15|20|30), delivery_format, style?, text_motion? (hold|breathe), prompt?, schedule_music_network?
POST /api/schedule/storyboard   + schedule_image_network, schedule_storyboard_network (JPEG/PNG), layer_overrides?, note?  -> suggested settings + overrides
GET  /api/schedule/progress/<job_id>
GET  /api/schedule/items
POST /api/schedule/items/<id>/send   {destination_id, filename?}

    Storyboard

    Pick a storyboard picture (JPEG or PNG) beside the artwork. The AI model reads it together with the artwork’s layers and sets the style, timing, length and each layer’s animation, then lists what it chose, why, and anything on the sketch it could not match to a layer or the animator cannot do. Everything is applied as ordinary settings, so it can be undone, changed layer by layer, previewed and saved as a look. Typed notes on the storyboard read more reliably than drawn arrows. It needs the AI model service (Ollama); without it, set things by hand as before.

    Sending

    Each plug has a Send control for the video destinations set up under Config > Network. The box beside it is the filename the copy gets there, filled in with the plug’s own name — change it to rename the file as it is sent. The extension is fixed to the delivery file’s own; spaces become underscores and characters that are not safe on a network share are dropped. The saved plug and its Download keep the original name, and a file of the same name already at the destination is replaced.

    Media & Library

    Upload or network folder

    Every media input can be a direct upload or Browse library on the configured Windows/SMB share:

    FieldNetwork folderFile types
    Main video, title/end cardHIRESVideo
    Background MusicMUSICAudio
    VO / narration, card VOVOAudio
    SFXSFXAudio

    Each category is configured in Config > Network (admin) with its own path and credentials. Network picks are copied into the work folder like uploads.

    Job monitor & saved videos

    • Job monitor (Your jobs) — your active, queued, and recent highlights video jobs with live progress. Vertical Shorts and Artwork Animation jobs are not listed here: each shows its progress in its own tab. The Dashboard counts all of yours together, and admins see every job of every kind under Jobs.
    • Saved videos — finished renders kept until deleted; reopen video, download, and scene breakdown.

    Player format compatibility

    The Player streams directly when the browser can decode the file. Broadcast masters (ProRes, DNxHD, many MXF) may fail in-browser; the Player then calls POST /api/media/playable to transcode to H.264/AAC MP4 and caches the result. Conversion applies to library picks, not local-only files.

    Tools

    Text to SFX

    One-shot effects via Woosh from a concrete description (e.g. "glass shattering"). Duration is enforced locally with ffmpeg. No silent fallback — if Woosh is down, the tool reports failure (the promo pipeline still has a procedural click for cut stamps).

    POST /api/sfx/generate  + prompt, duration, samples

    AI Assistant

    Chat over installed Ollama models. Optional app-knowledge system prompt helps with product questions. History is per-account. Attachments: images (vision models) and documents (server text extraction for PDF/text).

    GET  /api/chat/models
POST /api/chat/extract_file  + file
POST /api/chat  + model, messages, system?, think?

    Templates

    A template is a full programme setup: rating mode, duration, genre, transitions, audio targets, narration settings, plus music/SFX/VO/cards.

    Building

    Configure the form, attach assets, name it under Save as template. Saving an existing name updates settings and only rewrites slots you supply.

    Using

    Pick from the Template dropdown. Explicit form choices always win for that job. Delete removes stored assets; finished plugs stay in the library.

    GET/POST /api/templates
DELETE /api/templates/<id>
GET /api/templates/<id>/asset/<slot>
POST /api/trailer/generate + template_id

    Genre Presets

    Each genre sets a default transition, crossfade, SFX-at-cuts, and AI music/SFX themes.

    {% for g in genre_rows %} {% endfor %}
    GenreTransitionCrossfadeSFXMusic themeSFX theme
    {{ g.genre }} {{ g.transition }} {{ g.xfade_dur }}s {{ 'yes' if g.sfx else 'no' }} {{ g.music_theme }} {{ g.sfx_theme }}

    Music & VO tips

    ACE-Step lyrics

    • Thinking mode is off; vocal-suppressing negatives are dropped when lyrics are present.
    • Aim for ~2–3 words/sec (about 60–90 words for 30s). Keep lines short (4–8 words).
    • Use [verse] / [chorus] / [bridge] structure tags.

    Fish Audio delivery tags

    S2 uses square brackets ([happy]); older S1 uses parentheses. Place emotion at the start of a sentence; stack at most two tags.

    [confident] Tonight, the story everyone is talking about.
This is [emphasis] the one you cannot miss.

    Access & Theme

    Theme

    Rail controls: light / dark / auto (follows OS). Stored in aimp_theme localStorage per browser.

    Access control

    • Per-user accounts in the PostgreSQL users table; admins manage users under Config.
    • First-run default admin can be overridden with ADMIN_USERNAME / ADMIN_PASSWORD.
    • RESET_ADMIN=1 resets the admin password on boot — remove after use.
    • Login and file-route rate limits protect against brute force and enumeration.

    Session lifetime is SESSION_LIFETIME_DAYS (default 30). Cookie is Secure only when FORCE_HTTPS=1.

    {% endif %}

    Jobs

    All jobs across every account and every feature — highlights videos, Vertical Shorts and Artwork Animations share one queue. Cancel active or queued work from here.

    When every slot is busy, waiting jobs start by priority, then in the order they came in. Highlights videos and Artwork Animations start at High, Vertical Shorts at Normal; change a waiting job’s priority from its menu under Queued (Urgent puts it first). A job already running is never stopped for another.

    AI Service Configuration

    These control where the app looks for each local/self-hosted AI service. Changes save immediately (no restart needed) and are written to ai_services_config.json next to the script, so they persist across restarts too. Environment variables set the initial defaults; anything saved here overrides them from then on.

    Delivery-spec and tuning values that should be identical on every promo this deployment renders — broadcast loudness compliance, the house mix standard, and scene-detection tuning. Moved off the generator form so operators aren't asked about them on every job. Takes effect on the next render; no restart needed.

    Where Browse Library looks for source files (HIRES, cards, music, VO, SFX). Each category is fully independent — its own full network path, username, and password — since these often live on genuinely different volumes with different credentials. Takes effect immediately; no restart needed. Delivery destinations for "Send to destination" are managed separately below — a facility can configure several, each with its own name and format.

    Delivery destinations

    Named "Send to destination" targets, shown as a dropdown when delivering a finished render — a facility can configure several (e.g. separate Vantage watch folders, or a MAM ingest and a logging system side by side). Each has its own network path, credentials, and delivery format: the rendered video, the scene-list CSV, both, or an FCP XML rough-cut package (multi-material: HIRES video plus any surviving music/VO/card assets, transitions, cut-point markers, and optionally audio tracks) together with the original media it references.

    Branding

    Changes the name, tagline, footer, color theme, logo, and favicon everyone signed in (and the sign-in page itself) sees — saved to branding_config.json next to the script (text) and a branding/ folder in the plug library (logo/favicon files), so both persist across restarts. Takes effect immediately; existing sessions pick it up on their next page load.

    Shown at the very bottom of the sidebar, and on the sign-in page. Leave blank for no footer at all — most installs won't want one.

    Off: the address opens straight on the sign-in box (with Request access), without the product page behind it. Signed-in users are not affected.

    A coordinated set of colors used app-wide — the active-tab highlight, most buttons, badges, and status indicators, in both light and dark mode, including the sign-in page. Pick "Custom" to set just the accent color instead.

    Using the built-in default

    SVG, PNG, JPG, WEBP, or GIF. Displayed at 28×28 in the sidebar, so anything reasonably square works best.

    Using the built-in default

    ICO, SVG, or PNG. Browsers cache favicons aggressively — a hard refresh may be needed to see a change.
